title: XERODERMA PIGMENTOSUM, VARIANT TYPE
alt_titles: XERODERMA PIGMENTOSUM WITH NORMAL DNA REPAIR RATES

intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that the variant type of xeroderma pigmentosum (XPV) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the gene encoding DNA polymerase eta (POLH; hRAD30).

checks.claim: The variant type of xeroderma pigmentosum (XPV) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the gene encoding DNA polymerase eta (POLH; hRAD30).
checks.evidence_quote: We found that all XP-V cells examined carry mutations in their DNA polymerase eta gene.
checks.explanation: The abstract supports POLH mutations as the cause of XPV but does not say whether they are homozygous or compound heterozygous.

paragraphs.text: Xeroderma pigmentosum variant (XPV) is an inherited disorder associated with clinical photosensitivity and a higher rate of sunlight-induced skin cancers (Masutani et al., 1999; Itoh et al., 2000). Cells from most patients with xeroderma pigmentosum cannot excise ultraviolet (UV)-induced pyrimidine dimers from their DNA. XPV cells are different: they carry out nucleotide excision repair normally but cannot replicate UV-damaged DNA properly (Lehmann et al., 1975; Masutani et al., 1999). The disorder is caused by defects in DNA polymerase eta, which copies DNA past UV photoproducts (translesion synthesis) (Masutani et al., 1999; Johnson et al., 1999; Despras et al., 2010).

paragraphs.text: The term 'pigmented xerodermoid' was first used for a condition with mild clinical symptoms that seemed similar to, but separate from, xeroderma pigmentosum. Cleaver et al. (1980) compared UV-irradiated cell cultures and found that a pigmented xerodermoid culture could not be told apart from the XP variant in tests of unscheduled DNA synthesis, strand breakage during repair, chain growth during semiconservative DNA replication with or without caffeine, and recovery of DNA replication. They concluded that the term 'pigmented xerodermoid' was redundant.

paragraphs.text: Wang et al. (1991) noted that patients with XP variant have the clinical features of xeroderma pigmentosum, including more frequent skin cancers. However, their cells repair UV-induced DNA damage by nucleotide excision at a normal or nearly normal rate and are only slightly more sensitive than normal cells to being killed by UV.

paragraphs.text: Fujiwara et al. (1981) studied an 8-year-old boy (UV81KO) whose only symptom was acute recurrent sunburn, with no other physical or neuromental retardation. His skin had lowered minimal erythema doses between 280 and 300 nm, and erythema did not peak late. His cultured skin fibroblasts were 5-fold more sensitive to killing by 254-nm UV than normal cells. They were also more sensitive to fluorescent sunlamp (UV-B) radiation, 4-nitroquinoline-1-oxide, and N-hydroxy-acetyl aminofluorene, but not to mitomycin C or alkylating agents. Cells from obligate heterozygotes responded normally. No defect was found in nucleotide excision repair or in replicative bypass, including the increase in molecular weight of pulse-chased DNA. However, the cells did not recover DNA synthesis normally after 254-nm UV irradiation. The baseline sister chromatid exchange rate was raised (10 to 12 per cell compared with 5 per cell in normal cells). Fujiwara et al. (1981) proposed that the UV81KO disorder was a new photodermatosis, separate from xeroderma pigmentosum, Cockayne syndrome, and Bloom syndrome.

paragraphs.text: Lehmann et al. (1975) found that XP cells with normal excision repair synthesized DNA abnormally after UV irradiation. In irradiated cells, newly made DNA starts out at low molecular weight and is later converted to high molecular weight. This conversion took much longer in the variant cells than in normal cells. Caffeine strongly inhibited the slow conversion in variant cells but had no effect in normal cells. Two excision repair-deficient XP cell lines showed intermediate effects on both measures.

paragraphs.text: Cleaver et al. (1980) proposed that the defect shared by XP variant and pigmented xerodermoid cells was the loss of a gene product that lets normal cells replicate DNA without stopping at UV-induced pyrimidine dimers. Without it, replication forks in XP variant cells were blocked more often and at lower UV doses.

paragraphs.text: Wang et al. (1991) introduced a UV-irradiated shuttle vector carrying the supF target gene into an XP variant cell line. The mutation frequency rose linearly with dose, with a slope 5 times steeper than in normal cells. Of 53 independent mutants, 52 had base substitutions, and 62 of 64 substitutions involved a dipyrimidine. In XP variant cells, 28% of mutations involved A:T base pairs, compared with 11% in normal cells; most of these were at position 136. Wang et al. (1991) suggested that XP variant cells are less likely than normal cells to insert dAMP opposite photoproducts, which could explain why UV causes more mutations in these cells.

checks.explanation: Transfection is a way of introducing the vector, so the claim matches.

paragraphs.text: Itoh et al. (2000) reported that cells from heterozygous parents of XPV patients had normal unscheduled DNA synthesis and normal recovery of RNA and replicative DNA synthesis. In the presence of 1 mM caffeine, however, their recovery of replicative DNA synthesis was reduced to 53 +/- 8% of the normal control. In colony-forming assays, heterozygous cells survived UV normally without caffeine but survived slightly less well with 1 mM caffeine. The authors suggested that XPV heterozygotes could be identified by their UV sensitivity in the presence of nontoxic levels of caffeine.

paragraphs.text: Masutani et al. (1999) used a cell-free assay for translesion DNA synthesis to purify a DNA polymerase from HeLa cells that could continue replication past UV-induced thymine dimers in XPV cell extracts. They identified it as the human homolog of yeast Rad30, DNA polymerase eta (POLH). All XPV cells they examined carried mutations in the POLH gene. Recombinant human polymerase eta restored the ability of XPV cell extracts to replicate past thymine dimers on damaged DNA.

paragraphs.text: Despras et al. (2010) used DNA combing to show that, in UV-irradiated human cells lacking polymerase eta, far fewer replication forks were active and many forks were stalled. Large regions of single-stranded DNA formed during replication in irradiated XPV cells, which overactivated the ATR/CHK1 pathway after low UVC doses. A low concentration of caffeine given after irradiation reduced CHK1 activation and stopped DNA synthesis in XPV cells. Blocking CHK1 with UCN-01 made fork stalling worse in XPV cells and made them more sensitive to UVC, as caffeine does. The authors concluded that polymerase eta allows stalled forks to restart, and that without it CHK1 becomes essential for restarting replication by other pathways that stabilize the forks.

checks.evidence_quote: In the absence of poleta, Chk1 kinase becomes essential for replication resumption by alternative pathways, via fork stabilization.

paragraphs.text: XPV had been diagnosed from clinical findings together with a postreplication repair assay of the patient's cells. Itoh et al. (1996) described a simpler autoradiographic method that measures 3 markers after UV irradiation: unscheduled DNA synthesis, recovery of RNA synthesis, and recovery of replicative DNA synthesis. Each was compared with normal control cells. Among the hereditary photosensitive disorders, including other forms of xeroderma pigmentosum, Cockayne syndrome, and UV-sensitive syndrome, only XPV cells had normal unscheduled DNA synthesis and normal recovery of RNA synthesis but reduced recovery of replicative DNA synthesis (about 50% of control). Caffeine made this reduction greater. Because each disorder gave a different combination of the 3 markers, the method could also be used to tell these diseases apart.

checks.claim: XPV had been diagnosed from clinical findings together with a postreplication repair assay of the patient's cells.
checks.evidence_quote: Patients with xeroderma pigmentosum variant have been diagnosed based on a post-replication repair assay using their cells together with their clinical manifestations.

checks.claim: Itoh et al. (1996) described a simpler autoradiographic method for diagnosis that measures unscheduled DNA synthesis, recovery of RNA synthesis, and recovery of replicative DNA synthesis after UV irradiation, each compared with normal control cells.
checks.evidence_quote: an alternative simple method for the diagnosis of xeroderma pigmentosum variant that measures three cellular markers for DNA repair by autoradiography, unscheduled DNA synthesis, recovery of RNA synthesis, and recovery of replicative DNA synthesis after ultraviolet irradiation
checks.explanation: The abstract names the 3 markers and says each is compared with adjacent normal cells.

checks.claim: Itoh et al. (1996) found that among hereditary photosensitive disorders, including other forms of xeroderma pigmentosum, Cockayne syndrome, and UV-sensitive syndrome, only XPV cells had normal unscheduled DNA synthesis and normal recovery of RNA synthesis but reduced recovery of replicative DNA synthesis.
checks.evidence_quote: Of the hereditary photosensitive disorders including xeroderma pigmentosum, Cockayne syndrome, and newly established ultraviolet-sensitive syndrome, only xeroderma pigmentosum variant cells exhibit normal unscheduled DNA synthesis, normal recovery of RNA synthesis, but reduced recovery of replicative DNA synthesis

checks.claim: Itoh et al. (1996) found that recovery of replicative DNA synthesis in XPV cells was about 50% of control.
checks.evidence_quote: reduced recovery of replicative DNA synthesis (approximately 50% of that of control cells)
checks.explanation: The abstract gives the same figure.

checks.claim: Itoh et al. (1996) found that caffeine made the reduction in recovery of replicative DNA synthesis in XPV cells greater.
checks.evidence_quote: This reduction of DNA synthesis is enhanced in the presence of caffeine.

checks.claim: Itoh et al. (1996) found that each hereditary photosensitive disorder gave a different combination of the 3 markers, so the method could be used to tell these diseases apart.
checks.evidence_quote: Because each disorder yields a different combination of these three markers, this method also provides a systematic basis for the diagnosis of these diseases.

paragraphs.text: Using this method, Itoh et al. (2000) found that recovery of replicative DNA synthesis in XPV cells was 51 +/- 6% of normal controls, falling to 36 +/- 5% in the presence of a nontoxic level of caffeine.

checks.claim: Itoh et al. (2000) found that recovery of replicative DNA synthesis in XPV cells was 51 +/- 6% of normal controls.
checks.evidence_quote: only xeroderma pigmentosum variant cells exhibited normal unscheduled DNA synthesis, normal recovery of RNA synthesis, but reduced recovery of replicative DNA synthesis (51 +/- 6% the rate relative to normal controls)

checks.claim: Itoh et al. (2000) found that recovery of replicative DNA synthesis in XPV cells fell to 36 +/- 5% of normal controls in the presence of a nontoxic level of caffeine.
checks.evidence_quote: This reduction of recovery of replicative DNA synthesis was enhanced in the presence of a nontoxic level of caffeine to 36 +/- 5%.

clinical_synopsis.feature: Defective replication of UV-damaged DNA (postreplication repair defect) with normal nucleotide excision repair
Increased incidence of sunlight-induced skin cancers

paragraphs.text: In a Japanese patient with XPV, Itoh et al. (2000) found compound heterozygous mutations in the POLH gene. One was a 1840A-G transition causing a lys535-to-glu (K535E) substitution, and the other was a 2003A-C transversion causing a missense change at lys589. The patient had inherited the 2 mutations from heterozygous parents. Neither mutation was found in 52 unrelated Japanese individuals.

checks.claim: Itoh et al. (2000) found compound heterozygous mutations in the POLH gene in a Japanese patient with XPV.
checks.evidence_quote: In one family, we confirmed inheritance of two heterozygous mis-sense mutations.
checks.explanation: Compound heterozygosity is implied. The abstract does not name POLH and does not say the patient was Japanese; only the controls are described as Japanese.

checks.claim: One POLH mutation in the Japanese XPV patient was a 1840A-G transition causing a lys535-to-glu (K535E) substitution.
checks.evidence_quote: One mutation is an A-->G transition at nucleotide 1840 that generates a K535E mis-sense mutation.
checks.explanation: The mutation details match, but the abstract names neither the POLH gene nor the patient's ethnicity.

checks.claim: The other POLH mutation in the Japanese XPV patient was a 2003A-C transversion causing a missense change at lys589.
checks.evidence_quote: Another mutation is an A-->C transversion at nucleotide 2003 that generates a K589 mis-sense mutation.
checks.explanation: The mutation details match, but the abstract names neither the POLH gene nor the patient's ethnicity.

checks.claim: The Japanese XPV patient inherited the 2 POLH mutations from heterozygous parents.
checks.evidence_quote: In one family, we confirmed inheritance of two heterozygous mis-sense mutations.
checks.explanation: The abstract states the inheritance and that the parents were heterozygous.

checks.claim: Neither the POLH K535E nor the 2003A-C (lys589) mutation was found in 52 unrelated Japanese individuals.
checks.evidence_quote: Each of these mutations were absent in 52 unrelated Japanese individuals.

paragraphs.text: For discussion of the 2003A-C transversion in the POLH gene, which causes a missense change at lys589 and was found in compound heterozygous state in a patient with XPV by Itoh et al. (2000), see POLH, LYS535GLU.

checks.explanation: The variant matches, but the abstract does not name the POLH gene.

checks.claim: Itoh et al. (2000) found the POLH 2003A-C transversion in compound heterozygous state in a patient with XPV.

checks.explanation: The abstract implies compound heterozygosity in the patient but does not name the POLH gene.
